absent: Locking and concurrency rules for register tables and vcpu state.
Definitions and side effects of referenced access handlers for cache, TLBI, address translation, PMU, timers, GIC and debug controls.
Layouts of descriptor, parameter and vcpu structures and private data conventions.
Semantics of hidden-register checks, table search, tracing, program-counter helpers and undefined injection.
Full enumeration of instruction and coprocessor encodings beyond the groupings shown.

findings.text: Guest CP14 load and store traps are not emulated; the handler unconditionally injects an undefined instruction exception into the vcpu and reports the trap as handled.

Register access follows a fixed pipeline: emit a trace record with program counter and parameters, reject registers hidden by runtime configuration with undefined injection, treat a missing handler as a host bug path, otherwise invoke the descriptor handler and advance guest program counter only when the handler reports success.

Table-driven emulation returns not-handled when no table is supplied, otherwise searches the supplied table for the decoded parameters; on a hit it performs the access and reports handled, on a miss it reports not-handled without further side effects.

Unsupported coprocessor accesses map the trapped exception class to a coprocessor number, with two classes each mapping to fourteen and fifteen, log a diagnostic with program counter and status, and inject undefined; any other class takes a host warning path.

Sixty-four-bit coprocessor handling decodes direction and register selectors from the syndrome, builds a single sixty-four-bit operand from two thirty-two-bit guest registers, delegates to the supplied global register table, and on a successful read splits the resulting value back into the same two registers; a miss takes the unsupported-access path while still reporting handled.

CP10 identification traps are translated into AArch64 system register parameters with a fixed high exception level encoding and media control encoding; only reads are accepted, three identifier values select three media and vector feature registers, all other values or any write are rejected with an unimplemented diagnostic.

CP10 identification entry rejects untranslatable syndromes by injecting undefined, otherwise attempts system register emulation and on success writes the emulated value into the destination guest register; it always reports handled.

System register emulation searches the global AArch64 descriptor table; a hit performs the access and reports handled, a miss logs program counter and status, injects undefined, and reports not-handled.

CP15 identification emulation treats any write as unsupported, reports zero for encodings whose control field exceeds three to avoid future conflicts, otherwise delegates to system register emulation and writes the result to the destination register.

The instruction table binds cache set-way forms to access_dcsw and guarded forms to access_dcgsw, stage-one translation probes to handle_at_s1e01 with stage-two and combined forms to handle_at_s1e2 and handle_at_s12, EL1 invalidations to handle_tlbi_el1, EL2 invalidations to handle_tlbi_el2, all-EL1 forms to handle_alle1is, combined-stage forms to handle_vmalls12e1is, and IPA stage-two forms to handle_ipas2e1is and handle_ripas2e1is.

The debug identifier trap ignores writes through the shared ignore routine and synthesizes reads from the debug feature register and EL3 presence, packing watchpoint, breakpoint, context comparator and version subfields into upper positions with a fixed bit and EL3-derived bits lower down.

Per-index debug macros expand to four breakpoint and watchpoint value and control descriptors sharing one watchpoint trap with the index as private data, plus a separate extended breakpoint value descriptor with high-half mapping sharing the same trap.

The CP14 table provides sixteen sets of breakpoint and watchpoint entries through the per-index macro plus extended values through the second macro, maps identifier, communication, control, vector catch and authentication status registers to dedicated traps, and maps address, device, claim and miscellaneous debug registers to read-as-zero write-ignored behavior.
The sixty-four-bit CP14 table contains only two debug address range entries, both using read-as-zero write-ignored handling.

CP15 PMU encoding helpers attach visibility control to each descriptor and derive control fields from the counter index by splitting high and low bits, with separate helpers for counter values and type selectors.

The 32-bit CP15 table routes cache identity, control, translation, fault and memory attribute accesses to generic handlers with AArch64 backing registers, cache set-way operations to the cache handler, PMU control plus thirty-one counter and type entries to PMU handlers, timers to the arch timer handler, cache selection to dedicated handlers, and interrupt controller accesses mostly to undefined except directory and enable forms.

The sixty-four-bit CP15 table maps translation base halves to the generic VM handler, one PMU access to the counter handler, three interrupt software-generated forms to the SGI handler, and physical and virtual counter plus timer compare forms to the arch timer handler.
A descriptor with no handler after visibility checks is treated as a host programming error and diverted to a bad-trap diagnostic rather than advancing the guest.
An unexpected trap class reaching the unsupported-access path triggers a host warning before undefined injection, indicating an incomplete class mapping.

Sixty-four-bit trap decoding takes direction from syndrome bit zero, second register selector from bits ten to fourteen, low control field from bits one to four, and first opcode from bits sixteen to nineteen, with outer opcode zero and remaining decoded fields zeroed before table lookup.

CP10 identification uses syndrome bits ten to thirteen as identifier, accepting values seven, six and five for three feature registers with fixed outer opcode three and inner fields selecting media control, and low opcodes zero, one and two respectively.
